questions.question: A thermodynamic system is taken through cyclic process. The total work done in the process is :
questions.explanation:
For a cyclic process represented on a P-V diagram, the total work done is equal to the area enclosed by the cycle. Since the cycle C-D-E-C is clockwise, the work done is positive.

The given cycle forms a triangle with vertices at C(2, 100), D(2, 400), and E(4, 100).

The base of the triangle can be taken along the line connecting C and E, which is parallel to the V-axis. The length of the base is \(V_E - V_C = 4 - 2 = 2\) \(m^3\).

The height of the triangle is the perpendicular distance from D to the line CE, which is parallel to the P-axis. The height is \(P_D - P_C = 400 - 100 = 300\) \(Pa\).

The work done \(W\) is the area of the triangle:

$$
W = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}
$$

$$
W = \frac{1}{2} \times (V_E - V_C) \times (P_D - P_C)
$$

$$
W = \frac{1}{2} \times (4 - 2) \times (400 - 100)
$$

$$
W = \frac{1}{2} \times (2) \times (300)
$$

questions.question: The internal energy of a monoatomic gas is $3nRT$. One mole of helium is kept in a cylinder having internal cross section area of $17$ cm$^2$ and fitted with a light movable frictionless piston. The gas is heated slowly by suppling $126$ J heat. If the temperature rises by $4 ^\circ$C, then the piston will move $ \_\_\_\_ $ cm. (atmospheric pressure = $10^5$ Pa)
questions.explanation:
Given, internal energy of a monoatomic gas is \(U = 3nRT\).

Change in internal energy is given by:

$$
\Delta U = 3nR\Delta T
$$

Given \(n = 1\) mole, \(\Delta T = 4\) \(^\circ\)C. Assuming \(R = \frac{25}{3}\) J/mol K (as implied by the calculation in the solution):

$$
\Delta U = 3 \times 1 \times \frac{25}{3} \times 4 = 100 \text{ Joule}
$$

Heat supplied \(\Delta Q = 126\) J.

According to the first law of thermodynamics:

$$
\Delta Q = \Delta U + W
$$

Where \(W\) is the work done by the gas.

$$
126 = 100 + W
$$

$$
W = 26 \text{ Joule}
$$

Work done by the gas is also given by \(W = P\Delta V\).

$$
W = P(A\Delta x)
$$

Given atmospheric pressure \(P = 10^5\) Pa and cross-sectional area \(A = 17\) cm\(^2 = 17 \times 10^{-4}\) m\(^2\).

$$
26 = 10^5 \times 17 \times 10^{-4} \Delta x
$$

$$
26 = 17 \times 10 \Delta x
$$

$$
26 = 170 \Delta x
$$

Therefore, the displacement \(\Delta x\) is:

$$
\Delta x = \frac{26}{170} \text{ m}
$$

$$
\Delta x = 0.1529 \text{ m}
$$

Converting to cm:

$$
\Delta x = 0.1529 \times 100 \text{ cm}
$$

$$
\Delta x \approx 15.3 \text{ cm}
$$

questions.question: The magnitude of heat exchanged by a system for the given cyclic process ABCA (as shown in figure) is (in SI unit)
questions.explanation:
For a cyclic process, the heat exchanged \(Q\) is equal to the work done \(W\) by the system, i.e., \(Q = W\). The work done is the area enclosed by the cycle on the P-V diagram.

The given cyclic process ABCA encloses a semi-circular area. The diameter along the pressure axis is \(400 - 200 = 200\) k Pa, so the radius \(R_P = \frac{200}{2} = 100\) k Pa. The diameter along the volume axis is \(400 - 200 = 200\) cc, so the radius \(R_V = \frac{200}{2} = 100\) cc.

The work done \(W\) (area of the semi-circle) is given by:

$$
W = \frac{1}{2} \pi R_P R_V
$$

Converting units to SI:

• \(R_P = 100\) k Pa \(= 100 \times 10^3\) Pa
• \(R_V = 100\) cc \(= 100 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^3\)

$$
W = \frac{1}{2} \times \pi \times (\frac{200}{2} \times 10^3) \times (\frac{200}{2} \times 10^{-6})
$$

$$
W = \frac{1}{2} \times \pi \times (100 \times 10^3) \times (100 \times 10^{-6})
$$

$$
W = \frac{1}{2} \times \pi \times 10^5 \times 10^{-4}
$$

$$
W = \frac{1}{2} \times \pi \times 10
$$

$$
W = 5\pi \text{ J}
$$

Since \(Q = W\) for a cyclic process, the magnitude of heat exchanged is \(5\pi\) J.

questions.question: An engine operating between the boiling and freezing points of water will have • A. efficiency more than 27% • B. efficiency less than the efficiency of a Carnot engine operating between the same two temperatures. • C. efficiency equal to 27% • D. efficiency less than 27% Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
Engine is operating between FP and BP of water.

We need to find the efficiency of a Carnot engine operating between these temperatures.

$$
T_{1} = 100^{\circ}\text{C} \implies 100 + 273 = 373 \text{ K}
$$

$$
T_{2} = 0^{\circ}\text{C} \implies 0 + 273 = 273 \text{ K}
$$

We know the efficiency of a Carnot engine is given by:

$$
\eta = 1 - \frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}
$$

$$
\eta = 1 - \frac{273}{373}
$$

$$
\eta = \frac{373 - 273}{373} = \frac{100}{373}
$$

$$
\eta \approx 0.268
$$

Converting to percentage:

$$
\eta\% = 0.268 \times 100
$$

$$
\eta\% = 26.8\%
$$

Now let's evaluate the given statements based on this Carnot efficiency and the understanding that a real engine's efficiency is less than or equal to the Carnot efficiency.

• A. efficiency more than 27% (False, as \(26.8\% \lt 27\%\))
• B. efficiency less than the efficiency of a Carnot engine operating between the same two temperatures. (True, for any real engine, its efficiency \(\eta_{\text{real}} \lt \eta_{\text{Carnot}}\). The question refers to 'An engine', implying a general or real engine.)
• C. efficiency equal to 27% (False, as \(26.8\% \ne 27\%\))
• D. efficiency less than 27% (True, as \(26.8\% \lt 27\%\). Since \(\eta_{\text{real}} \le 26.8\%\), it will always be less than 27%.)

Therefore, statements B and D are correct.

questions.question: A sample of gas at temperature T is adiabatically expanded to double its volume. Adiabatic constant for the gas is $\gamma = 3/2$. The work done by the gas in the process is : ($\mu = 1$ mole)
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Given initial temperature \(T_1 = T\), initial volume \(V_1 = V\), final volume \(V_2 = 2V\), adiabatic constant \(\gamma = 3/2\), and number of moles \(n = 1\).

For an adiabatic process, the relation between temperature and volume is \(TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{constant}\).

$$
T_1 V_1^{\gamma-1} = T_2 V_2^{\gamma-1}
$$

Substitute the given values:

$$
T \cdot V^{\gamma-1} = T_2 \cdot (2V)^{\gamma-1}
$$

$$
T_2 = T \left(\frac{V}{2V}\right)^{\gamma-1} = T \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\gamma-1}
$$

Given \(\gamma = 3/2\), so \(\gamma-1 = 3/2 - 1 = 1/2\).

$$
T_2 = T \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{1/2} = \frac{T}{\sqrt{2}}
$$

The work done by the gas in an adiabatic process is given by:

$$
W = \frac{nR(T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1}
$$

Substitute \(n=1\), \(T_1=T\), \(T_2 = T/\sqrt{2}\), and \(\gamma-1 = 1/2\):

$$
W = \frac{1 \cdot R \left(T - \frac{T}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}{1/2}
$$

$$
W = 2R \left(T - \frac{T}{\sqrt{2}}\right)
$$

$$
W = 2RT \left(1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)
$$

$$
W = RT \left(2 - \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\right)
$$

$$
W = RT(2 - \sqrt{2})
$$

This matches option (4).

questions.question: In an adiabatic process, which of the following statements is true ?
options: The molar heat capacity is infinite
Work done by the gas equals the increase in internal energy
The molar heat capacity is zero
The internal energy of the gas decreases as the temperature increases
questions.explanation:
For adiabatic process, \(dQ = 0\)

Therefore, Molar heat capacity \(C = \frac{dQ}{n dT} = 0\)

Also, from the first law of thermodynamics, \(dQ = dU + dW\)

Since \(dQ = 0\), we have \(0 = dU + dW \Rightarrow dU = -dW\)

Also, for an ideal gas, \(dU = \frac{f}{2} nRdT\)

From the above, only option (3) is correct.

questions.question: During the melting of a slab of ice at 273 K at atmospheric pressure :
options: Internal energy of ice-water system remains unchanged.
Positive work is done by the ice-water system on the atmosphere.
Internal energy of the ice-water system decreases.
Positive work is done on the ice-water system by the atmosphere.
questions.explanation:
Volume decreases during melting of ice so positive work is done on ice water system by atmosphere.

Heat absorbed by ice water so \(\Delta Q\) is positive, work done by ice water system is negative.

Hence by first law of thermodynamics

$$
\Delta U = \Delta Q + \Delta W = \text{Positive}
$$

So internal energy increases.

questions.question: During an adiabatic process, if the pressure of a gas is found to be proportional to the cube of its absolute temperature, then the ratio of $\frac{C_{P}}{C_{V}}$ for the gas is :
Work done by a Carnot engine operating between temperatures $127^{\circ}C$ and $27^{\circ}C$ is $2$ kJ. The amount of heat transferred to the engine by the reservoir is:
questions.explanation:
Temperatures of the hot and cold reservoirs are \(T_{1} = 127^{\circ}C = 127 + 273 = 400\) K and \(T_{2} = 27^{\circ}C = 27 + 273 = 300\) K respectively.

Work done by the engine \(w = 2\) kJ.

$$
\eta = 1 - \frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}
$$

Substituting the values:

$$
\eta = 1 - \frac{300}{400} = 1 - \frac{3}{4} = \frac{1}{4}
$$

Also, efficiency is given by:

$$
\eta = \frac{w}{Q_{1}}
$$

Where \(Q_{1}\) is the heat transferred to the engine by the hot reservoir.

Equating the two expressions for efficiency:

$$
\frac{w}{Q_{1}} = \frac{1}{4}
$$

Substituting the value of work done \(w = 2\) kJ:

$$
\frac{2}{Q_{1}} = \frac{1}{4}
$$

$$
Q_{1} = 2 \times 4 = 8\text{ kJ}
$$

questions.question: An ideal gas exists in a state with pressure $P_0$, volume $V_0$. It is isothermally expanded to 4 times of its initial volume ($V_0$), then isobarically compressed to its original volume. Finally the system is heated isochorically to bring it to its initial state. The amount of heat exchanged in this process is :
questions.explanation:
The process involves three stages: isothermal expansion, isobaric compression, and isochoric heating, returning the gas to its initial state. This is a cyclic process.

For an isothermal expansion from \(V_0\) to \(4V_0\) at pressure \(P_0\) (initial state):

$$
\omega_1 = P_0 V_0 \ln\left(\frac{4V_0}{V_0}\right) = P_0 V_0 \ln4
$$

For an isobaric compression from \(4V_0\) to \(V_0\) at pressure \(P_0/4\):

$$
\omega_2 = P_0' (V_f - V_i) = \frac{P_0}{4} (V_0 - 4V_0) = \frac{P_0}{4} (-3V_0) = -\frac{3P_0 V_0}{4}
$$

For an isochoric heating from \(V_0\) to \(V_0\):

$$
\omega_3 = 0
$$

The total work done in the cyclic process is the sum of work done in each stage:

$$
\omega = \omega_1 + \omega_2 + \omega_3 = P_0 V_0 \ln4 - \frac{3P_0 V_0}{4} + 0
$$

$$
\omega = P_0 V_0 \left(\ln4 - \frac{3}{4}\right)
$$

For a cyclic process, the change in internal energy is zero (\(\Delta U_{\text{cyclic}} = 0\)). According to the first law of thermodynamics, the total heat exchanged \(Q_T\) is equal to the total work done \(\omega\):

$$
Q_T = \Delta U_{\text{cyclic}} + \omega
$$

$$
Q_T = 0 + \omega = \omega
$$

$$
Q_T = P_0 V_0 \left(\ln4 - \frac{3}{4}\right)
$$

We know that \(\ln4 = \ln(2^2) = 2\ln2\) and \(3/4 = 0.75\).

$$
Q_T = P_0 V_0 (2\ln2 - 0.75)
$$

questions.question: Given are statements for certain thermodynamic variables, (A) Internal energy, volume $V$ and mass $M$ are extensive variables. (B) Pressure $P$, temperature $T$ and density $\rho$ are intensive variables. (C) Volume $V$, temperature $T$ and density $\rho$ are intensive variables. (D) Mass $M$, temperature $T$ and internal energy are extensive variables. Choose the correct answer from the points given below :
questions.explanation:
Extensive variables depends on size or mass of system ex : internal energy, volume, mass

Intensive variables do not depend on the amount of matter, ex: pressure, temperature, density.

Let's evaluate each statement:

(A) Internal energy, volume \(V\) and mass \(M\) are extensive variables. (Correct)

(B) Pressure \(P\), temperature \(T\) and density \(\rho\) are intensive variables. (Correct)

(C) Volume \(V\), temperature \(T\) and density \(\rho\) are intensive variables. (Incorrect, Volume is extensive)

(D) Mass \(M\), temperature \(T\) and internal energy are extensive variables. (Incorrect, Temperature is intensive)

Therefore, statements (A) and (B) are correct.

questions.question: During an adiabatic process, the pressure of a gas is found to be proportional to the cube of its absolute temperature. The ratio of $\frac{C_{p}}{C_{v}}$ for the gas is:
questions.explanation:
Given \(P \propto T^{3} \Rightarrow P \propto \left(\frac{PV}{nR}\right)^{3}\)

\( \Rightarrow P^{2}V^{3} = \text{constant}\)

\( \Rightarrow PV^{3/2} = \text{constant}\)

for adiabatic \(PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}\)

\( \Rightarrow \gamma = \frac{C_{p}}{C_{v}} = \frac{3}{2}\)

questions.question: A total of 48 J heat is given to one mole of helium kept in a cylinder. The temperature of helium increases by 2°C. The work done by the gas is : (Given : R = 8.31 J k⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
$$
\Delta Q = 48J
$$

$$
\Delta U = \frac{nfR\Delta T}{2} = 1.\frac{3}{2}R(2) = 3R = 3 (8.3) = 24.9 J
$$

$$
\Delta Q = \omega + \Delta U
$$

$$
\omega = \Delta Q - \Delta U
$$

$$
\omega = 48 - 24.9
$$

$$
\omega = 23.1J
$$

questions.question: Given below are two statements. One is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A) : With the increase in the pressure of an ideal gas, the volume falls off more rapidly in an isothermal process in comparison to the adiabatic process. Reason (R) : In isothermal process, $PV = \text{constant}$, while in adiabatic process $PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$. Here $\gamma$ is the ratio of specific heats, P is the pressure and V is the volume of the ideal gas. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation:
From the P-V diagram for compression, the slope of the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal curve. This is represented by the inequality:

$$
\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{Adiabatic}} > \left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{Isothermal}}
$$

The magnitude of the slope \(|dP/dV|\) for an adiabatic process is \(\gamma\) times that for an isothermal process (since \(|dP/dV|_{\text{adiabatic}} = \gamma P/V\) and \(|dP/dV|_{\text{isothermal}} = P/V\), and \(\gamma > 1\)). A steeper slope means that for a given increase in pressure, the volume decreases less rapidly in an adiabatic process than in an isothermal process. Therefore, Assertion (A) is false.

Reason (R) correctly states the equations for isothermal process (\(PV = \text{constant}\)) and adiabatic process (\(PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}\)) and defines \(\gamma\) as the ratio of specific heats, P as pressure, and V as volume. So, Reason (R) is true.

Since Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is true, the correct option is (4).

questions.question: A Carnot engine operating between two reservoirs has efficiency $\frac{1}{3}$. When the temperature of cold reservoir raised by $x$, its efficiency decreases to $\frac{1}{6}$. The value of $x$, if the temperature of hot reservoir is $99^{\circ}C$, will be :
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Given initial efficiency \(\eta = \frac{1}{3}\).

When the temperature of the cold reservoir is raised by \(x\), the new temperature is \((T_{2} + x)\). The new efficiency is \(\eta' = \frac{1}{6}\).

The temperature of the hot reservoir is \(T_{1} = 99^{\circ}C\). Converting to Kelvin:

$$
T_{1} = 99 + 273 = 372K
$$

The efficiency of a Carnot engine is given by \(\eta = 1 - \frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}\).

Using the initial efficiency:

$$
\frac{1}{3} = 1 - \frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{3} = 1 - \frac{T_{2}}{372}
$$

$$
\frac{T_{2}}{372} = 1 - \frac{1}{3}
$$

$$
\frac{T_{2}}{372} = \frac{2}{3}
$$

$$
T_{2} = \frac{2}{3} \times 372
$$

$$
T_{2} = 2 \times 124
$$

$$
T_{2} = 248K
$$

The new efficiency \(\eta'\) is given by:

$$
\eta' = 1 - \frac{(T_{2} + x)}{T_{1}}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{6} = 1 - \frac{(248 + x)}{372}
$$

$$
\frac{(248 + x)}{372} = 1 - \frac{1}{6}
$$

$$
\frac{(248 + x)}{372} = \frac{5}{6}
$$

$$
248 + x = \frac{5}{6} \times 372
$$

$$
248 + x = 5 \times 62
$$

$$
248 + x = 310
$$

$$
x = 310 - 248
$$

$$
x = 62K
$$

questions.question: Consider two containers A and B containing monatomic gases at the same Pressure (P), Volume (V) and Temperature (T). The gas in A is compressed isothermally to $\frac{1}{8}$ of its original volume while the gas in B is compressed adiabatically to $\frac{1}{8}$ of its original volume. The ratio of final pressure of gas in B to that of gas in A is
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

For an isothermal process, the product of pressure and volume remains constant. Let the initial pressure be \(P\) and initial volume be \(V\). The final volume is \(V_{2A} = \frac{V}{8}\).

$$
P_{1}V_{1} = P_{2A}V_{2A}
$$

$$
PV = P_{2A} \left(\frac{V}{8}\right)
$$

$$
P_{2A} = 8P
$$

For a monatomic gas, the adiabatic index is \(\gamma = \frac{5}{3}\). For an adiabatic process, the relation between pressure and volume is given by: Let the initial pressure be \(P\) and initial volume be \(V\). The final volume is \(V_{2B} = \frac{V}{8}\).

$$
P_{1}V_{1}^{\gamma} = P_{2B}V_{2B}^{\gamma}
$$

$$
PV^{5/3} = P_{2B} \left(\frac{V}{8}\right)^{5/3}
$$

$$
P_{2B} = (8)^{5/3} P
$$

The ratio of final pressure of gas in B to that of gas in A is \(\frac{P_{2B}}{P_{2A}}\).

$$
\frac{P_{2B}}{P_{2A}} = \frac{(8)^{5/3} P}{8P}
$$

$$
\frac{P_{2B}}{P_{2A}} = 8^{(5/3) - 1}
$$

$$
\frac{P_{2B}}{P_{2A}} = 8^{2/3}
$$

$$
\frac{P_{2B}}{P_{2A}} = (2^3)^{2/3}
$$

$$
\frac{P_{2B}}{P_{2A}} = 2^2 = 4
$$

questions.question: Consider the following statements: • A. Zeroth law of thermodynamics gives concept of temperature • B. First law of thermodynamics gives concept of internal energy • C. In isothermal expansion of ideal gas, $\Delta Q \neq \Delta W$ • D. Product of intensive and extensive variables is extensive • E. The ratio of any extensive variable to mass will be an extensive variable Choose the correct combination of statements from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Let's analyze each statement:

• A. Zeroth law of thermodynamics defines temperature. This statement is TRUE.
• B. First law of thermodynamics defines internal energy. This statement is TRUE.
• C. For isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, the change in internal energy \(\Delta U = 0\). According to the first law of thermodynamics, \(\Delta U = \Delta Q - \Delta W\). Therefore, \(0 = \Delta Q - \Delta W\), which implies \(\Delta Q = \Delta W\). So, the statement \(\Delta Q \neq \Delta W\) is FALSE.
• D. The product of an intensive variable and an extensive variable is an extensive variable. For example, Pressure (intensive) \(\times\) Volume (extensive) = Work (extensive). This statement is TRUE.
• E. The ratio of two extensive variables is an intensive variable. For example, mass (extensive) / volume (extensive) = density (intensive). So, the ratio of any extensive variable to mass will be an intensive variable, not an extensive variable. Thus, this statement is FALSE.

Based on the analysis, statements A, B, and D are correct.

questions.question: Two different adiabatic paths for the same gas intersect two isothermal curves as shown in P-V diagram. The relation between the ratio $\frac{V_{a}}{V_{d}}$ and the ratio $\frac{V_{b}}{V_{c}}$ is:
questions.explanation:
For a Carnot cycle, which consists of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes, the following relationship between volumes holds true:

$$
V_{a}V_{c} = V_{b}V_{d}
$$

Rearranging the above equation to find the relation between the given ratios:

$$
\frac{V_{a}}{V_{d}} = \frac{V_{b}}{V_{c}}
$$

questions.question: Choose the correct statement for processes A & B shown in figure.
options: $PV^{\gamma} = k \text{ for process B and } PV = k \text{ for process A.}$
$PV = k \text{ for process B and } T = k \text{ for process A.}$
$\frac{P^{\gamma-1}}{T^{\gamma}} = k \text{ for process B and } T = k \text{ for process A.}$
$\frac{T^{\gamma}}{P^{\gamma-1}} = k \text{ for process A and } PV = k \text{ for process B.}$
questions.explanation:
The given figure shows two processes A and B on a P-V diagram. We need to identify the nature of these processes based on their slopes.

• For an isothermal process, \(PV = \text{constant}\). The slope is \(\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{iso}} = -\frac{P}{V}\).
• For an adiabatic process, \(PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}\). The slope is \(\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{adia}} = -\gamma\frac{P}{V}\).
• Since \(\gamma > 1\), the magnitude of the slope of an adiabatic curve is greater than that of an isothermal curve at any given point.
• From the diagram, the slope of curve A is less steep than the slope of curve B. Therefore, \((\text{Slope})_{A} \lt (\text{Slope})_{B}\).
• This implies that Process A is an isothermal process, for which \(PV = K\) (constant).
• And Process B is an adiabatic process, for which \(PV^{\gamma} = K\) (constant).

questions.question: The heat absorbed by a system in going through the given cyclic process is :
questions.explanation:
For a cyclic process, the heat absorbed \(\theta\) is equal to the net work done \(W\), which corresponds to the area enclosed by the cycle on the P-V diagram.

$$
\theta = W = \text{area enclosed}
$$

The area of the circular/elliptical path is given by \(\pi ab\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are the semi-axes. This can be calculated using the diameters \((2a\) and \(2b)\) along each axis.

$$
\theta = \pi ab = \frac{\pi(2a)(2b)}{4}
$$

From the graph, the diameter along the pressure axis is \(\Delta P = (340 - 60) \text{ kPa} = 280 \times 10^3 \text{ Pa}\). The diameter along the volume axis is \(\Delta V = (340 - 60) \text{ cc} = 280 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3\). Note: The axis labels in the diagram (P in cc, V in kPa) appear to be swapped; the calculation uses the standard convention of P in kPa and V in cc.

$$
\theta = \frac{\pi(280 \times 10^{3})(280 \times 10^{-6})}{4}
$$

$$
\theta = \frac{\pi(78.4)}{4} = 19.6\pi \approx 61.6 \, \text{J}
$$

questions.question: A gas is compressed adiabatically, which one of the following statement is NOT true.
options: There is no change in the internal energy
The temperature of the gas increases.
The change in the internal energy is equal to the work done on the gas
There is no heat supplied to the system
questions.explanation:
In an adiabatic process, there is no heat exchange with the surroundings, so the change in heat \(\Delta Q\) is zero.

$$
\Delta Q = 0
$$

When a gas is compressed, work is done on the gas. According to the sign convention where \(w\) is the work done by the gas, compression means \(w < 0\). Thus, work is not zero.

$$
w \neq 0
$$

According to the first law of thermodynamics:

$$
\Delta Q = \Delta u + w
$$

Substituting \(\Delta Q = 0\) for an adiabatic process:

$$
0 = \Delta u + w
$$

This gives the change in internal energy as:

$$
\Delta u = -w
$$

Since work \(w\) is done by the gas and is non-zero, the change in internal energy \(\Delta u\) is also non-zero. Therefore, the statement that there is no change in the internal energy is false.

questions.question: The specific heat at constant pressure of a real gas obeying $PV^2 = RT$ equations is :
questions.explanation:
dQ = du + dw

ncdT = ncvdT + dw

questions.question: A Carnot engine with efficiency 50% takes heat from a source at 600 K. In order to increase the efficiency to 70%, keeping the temperature of sink same, the new temperature of the source will be :
questions.explanation:
The efficiency of a Carnot engine is given by:

$$
\eta = 1 - \frac{T_L}{T_H}
$$

Given initial efficiency \(\eta_1 = 50\% = 0.5\) and source temperature \(T_H = 600\) K.

Using the formula to find the sink temperature \(T_L\):

$$
0.5 = 1 - \frac{T_L}{600}
$$

$$
\frac{T_L}{600} = 1 - 0.5
$$

$$
\frac{T_L}{600} = 0.5
$$

$$
T_L = 0.5 \times 600 K = 300 K
$$

Now, the efficiency is increased to \(\eta_2 = 70\% = 0.7\), and the sink temperature \(T_L\) remains the same (300 K). We need to find the new source temperature \(T_2\).

$$
0.7 = 1 - \frac{300}{T_2}
$$

$$
\frac{300}{T_2} = 1 - 0.7
$$

$$
\frac{300}{T_2} = 0.3
$$

$$
T_2 = \frac{300}{0.3}
$$

$$
T_2 = 1000 K
$$

Thus, the new temperature of the source will be 1000 K.

questions.question: The temperature of 1 mole of an ideal monoatomic gas is increased by 50°C at constant pressure. The total heat added and change in internal energy are $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$, respectively. If $\frac{E_{1}}{E_{2}} = \frac{x}{9}$ then the value of $x$ is _________.
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

For an ideal monoatomic gas, the degrees of freedom \(f = 3\).

The molar heat capacity at constant volume is \(C_{v} = \frac{f}{2}R = \frac{3}{2}R\).

The molar heat capacity at constant pressure is \(C_{p} = C_{v} + R = \frac{3}{2}R + R = \frac{5}{2}R\).

Given: Number of moles \(n = 1\).

The process occurs at constant pressure, and the temperature change is \(\Delta T = 50^{\circ}\text{C}\).

Total heat added (\(E_{1}\)) at constant pressure is given by:

$$
E_{1} = n C_{p} \Delta T = 1 \times \frac{5}{2}R \Delta T = \frac{5}{2}R \Delta T
$$

Change in internal energy (\(E_{2}\)) is given by:

$$
E_{2} = n C_{v} \Delta T = 1 \times \frac{3}{2}R \Delta T = \frac{3}{2}R \Delta T
$$

We are given the relation \(\frac{E_{1}}{E_{2}} = \frac{x}{9}\).

Substitute the expressions for \(E_{1}\) and \(E_{2}\) into the given ratio:

$$
\frac{\frac{5}{2}R \Delta T}{\frac{3}{2}R \Delta T} = \frac{x}{9}
$$

Simplify the left side:

$$
\frac{5}{3} = \frac{x}{9}
$$

Now, solve for \(x\):

$$
x = \frac{5}{3} \times 9
$$

$$
x = 5 \times 3
$$

$$
x = 15
$$

questions.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as **Assertion A** and the other is labelled as **Reason R** **Statement I** : Change in internal energy of a system containing n mole of ideal gas can be written as $\Delta U = nC_{V}(T_{f} - T_{i}) = \frac{nR}{\gamma-1}(T_{f} - T_{i})$, where $\gamma = \frac{C_{p}}{C_{V}}$, $T_{i} = $ initial temperature, $T_{f} = $ final temperature. **Statement II** : Relation between degree of freedom f and $\gamma (= C_{p}/C_{V})$ is  \left(\gamma = 1 + \frac{2}{f}\right)$$. Choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

The change in internal energy (\(\Delta U\)) for n moles of an ideal gas is defined in terms of the molar heat capacity at constant volume, \(C_{V}\), and the change in temperature, \(\Delta T = T_{f} - T_{i}\).

$$
\Delta U = nC_{V}(T_{f} - T_{i})
$$

This is the first part of the statement, which is correct.

Next, we use Mayer's relation for an ideal gas, \(C_{p} - C_{V} = R\), and the definition of the adiabatic index, \(\gamma = \frac{C_{p}}{C_{V}}\). From the definition of \(\gamma\), we have \(C_{p} = \gamma C_{V}\). Substituting this into Mayer's relation:

$$
\gamma C_{V} - C_{V} = R
$$

$$
C_{V}(\gamma - 1) = R
$$

$$
C_{V} = \frac{R}{\gamma - 1}
$$

Substituting this expression for \(C_{V}\) back into the equation for \(\Delta U\):

$$
\Delta U = n \left( \frac{R}{\gamma - 1} \right) (T_{f} - T_{i}) = \frac{nR}{\gamma - 1}(T_{f} - T_{i})
$$

This matches the second part of the statement. Therefore, Statement I is TRUE.

For an ideal gas with \(f\) degrees of freedom, the internal energy per mole is given by \(U_{m} = \frac{f}{2}RT\). The molar heat capacity at constant volume is the derivative of internal energy with respect to temperature:

$$
C_{V} = \frac{dU_{m}}{dT} = \frac{d}{dT} \left( \frac{f}{2}RT \right) = \frac{f}{2}R
$$

Using Mayer's relation, \(C_{p} = C_{V} + R\):

$$
C_{p} = \frac{f}{2}R + R = \left( \frac{f+2}{2} \right)R
$$

Now, we find the ratio \(\gamma\):

$$
\gamma = \frac{C_{p}}{C_{V}} = \frac{\left( \frac{f+2}{2} \right)R}{\frac{f}{2}R} = \frac{f+2}{f} = 1 + \frac{2}{f}
$$

This matches the relation given in the statement. Therefore, Statement II is also TRUE.

Both statements are correct physical relations. However, Statement I is a general thermodynamic relation derived from the definitions of \(C_{V}\), \(C_{p}\), and \(\gamma\), which are macroscopic properties. Statement II provides a link between the macroscopic property \(\gamma\) and the microscopic property of the gas (degrees of freedom, \(f\)).

The derivation of Statement I does not require Statement II. Statement I holds true for any ideal gas regardless of its degrees of freedom. Therefore, Statement II is not the correct explanation for Statement I.

questions.question: The workdone in an adiabatic change in an ideal gas depends upon only :
questions.explanation:
For an adiabatic process, the work done is given by the change in internal energy:

$$
\Delta W = -\Delta U
$$

For an ideal gas, the change in internal energy is directly proportional to the change in temperature:

$$
\Delta U = nC_{V}\Delta T
$$

Therefore, the work done in an adiabatic change in an ideal gas depends only on the change in its temperature:

$$
\Delta W = -nC_{V}\Delta T
$$

questions.question: The pressure of a gas changes linearly with volume from $A$ to $B$ as shown in figure. If no heat is supplied to or extracted from the gas then change in the internal energy of the gas will be
questions.explanation:
The work done \(W\) by the gas during a process shown on a \(P-V\) graph is the area under the curve. The process goes from state \(A\) to state \(B\). From the graph, the volume decreases from \(200\) cc to \(50\) cc, which means the gas is compressed. Therefore, the work done by the gas is negative.

The area under the curve is a trapezoid. The formula for the area of a trapezoid is \(\frac{1}{2} \times (\text{sum of parallel sides}) \times \text{height}\).

• Pressure at state A (\(V=200\) cc), \(P_A = 10\) KPa \(= 10 \times 10^3\) Pa
• Pressure at state B (\(V=50\) cc), \(P_B = 50\) KPa \(= 50 \times 10^3\) Pa
• Change in volume (height of trapezoid), \(\Delta V = V_A - V_B = 200\) cc \(- 50\) cc \(= 150\) cc \(= 150 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^3\)

The work done \(W\) by the gas is the negative of the area under the \(P-V\) curve:

$$
W = -\frac{1}{2} (P_A + P_B) \times (V_A - V_B)
$$

$$
W = -\frac{1}{2} (10 \times 10^3 \text{ Pa} + 50 \times 10^3 \text{ Pa}) \times (200 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3 - 50 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3)
$$

$$
W = -\frac{1}{2} (60 \times 10^3) \times (150 \times 10^{-6})
$$

$$
W = -(30 \times 10^3) \times (150 \times 10^{-6})
$$

$$
W = -4500 \times 10^{-3}
$$

$$
W = -4.5 \text{ J}
$$

The First Law of Thermodynamics states that \(Q = \Delta U + W\), where \(Q\) is the heat supplied to the system, \(\Delta U\) is the change in internal energy, and \(W\) is the work done by the system.

The problem states that no heat is supplied to or extracted from the gas, which means the process is adiabatic, so \(Q = 0\).

$$
0 = \Delta U + W
$$

$$
\Delta U = -W
$$

Substitute the calculated value of \(W\) into the equation:

$$
\Delta U = -(-4.5 \text{ J})
$$

$$
\Delta U = 4.5 \text{ J}
$$

questions.question: A gas of certain mass filled in a closed cylinder at a pressure of $3.23$ kPa has temperature $50^{\circ}\text{C}$. The gas is now heated to double its temperature. The modified pressure is $\text{______}$ Pa.
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

As per NTA (National Testing Agency) guidelines, the solution proceeds as follows:

For a gas in a closed cylinder, the volume (V) is constant.

$$
V = \text{constant}
$$

According to Gay-Lussac's Law, for a fixed mass of gas at constant volume, the pressure (P) is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (T).

$$
P \propto T
$$

This implies that the ratio of final pressure to initial pressure is equal to the ratio of final absolute temperature to initial absolute temperature:

$$
\frac{P_{f}}{P_{i}} = \frac{T_{f}}{T_{i}}
$$

Given initial temperature \(T_{i}\) and initial pressure \(P_{i}\):

$$
T_{i} = 50^{\circ}\text{C} = (50 + 273) \text{ K} = 323 \text{ K}
$$

$$
P_{i} = 3.23 \text{ kPa}
$$

The problem states the gas is heated to double its temperature. Following the interpretation used in the provided solution (doubling the Celsius temperature value):

$$
\text{New Celsius temperature} = 2 \times 50^{\circ}\text{C} = 100^{\circ}\text{C}
$$

Converting this to Kelvin for the final temperature \(T_{f}\):

$$
T_{f} = 100^{\circ}\text{C} = (100 + 273) \text{ K} = 373 \text{ K}
$$

Now, substitute the values into the Gay-Lussac's Law equation:

$$
\frac{P_{f}}{3.23 \text{ kPa}} = \frac{373 \text{ K}}{323 \text{ K}}
$$

Solve for \(P_{f}\):

$$
P_{f} = 3.23 \text{ kPa} \times \frac{373}{323}
$$

Convert kPa to Pa (\(1 \text{ kPa} = 1000 \text{ Pa}\)):

$$
P_{f} = (3.23 \times 1000) \text{ Pa} \times \frac{373}{323}
$$

$$
P_{f} = 3230 \text{ Pa} \times \frac{373}{323}
$$

$$
P_{f} \approx 3730 \text{ Pa}
$$

Thus, the modified pressure is approximately \(3730\) Pa.

If "double its temperature" were interpreted as doubling the absolute temperature (Kelvin), the calculation would be:

$$
T_{i} = 323 \text{ K}
$$

$$
T_{f} = 2 \times T_{i} = 2 \times 323 \text{ K} = 646 \text{ K}
$$

$$
P_{f} = 2 \times P_{i} = 2 \times 3.23 \text{ kPa} = 6.46 \text{ kPa} = 6460 \text{ Pa}
$$

However, the provided answer (3730) corresponds to the first interpretation (doubling the Celsius temperature).

questions.question: Given below are two statements. One is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason(R). Assertion (A) : In an insulated container, a gas is adiabatically shrunk to half of its initial volume. The temperature of the gas decreases. Reason (R) : Free expansion of an ideal gas is an irreversible and an adiabatic process. In the light of the above statement, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questions.explanation:
(A) For an adiabatic process, \(T_{1}V_{1}^{\gamma-1} = T_{2}V_{2}^{\gamma-1}\). When a gas is shrunk (compressed), its temperature increases. Therefore, Assertion (A) is false.

(R) Free expansion of an ideal gas is indeed an irreversible and adiabatic process by definition. Therefore, Reason (R) is true.

questions.question: A cylinder with adiabatic walls is closed at both ends and is divided into two compartments by a frictionless adiabatic piston. Ideal gas is filled in both (left and right) the compartments at same P,V, T. Heating is started from left side until pressure changes to $\frac{27P}{8}$. If initial volume of each compartment was 9 litres then the final volume in right-hand side compartment is ____ litres. (for this ideal gas $C_{p}/C_{V} = 1.5$)
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

The cylinder and piston are adiabatic. When the left compartment is heated, the gas in the right compartment is compressed. Since the process is slow (implied by equilibrium states) and the walls are adiabatic, the compression in the right compartment is an adiabatic process.

• Initial pressure in the right compartment, \(P_{i} = P\)
• Initial volume in the right compartment, \(V_{i} = 9\) litres
• Final pressure in the right compartment, \(P_{f} = \frac{27P}{8}\) (since the piston is frictionless, the final pressure is the same on both sides)
• The ratio of specific heats, \(\gamma = \frac{C_{p}}{C_{V}} = 1.5 = \frac{3}{2}\)

For an adiabatic process, the relationship between pressure and volume is given by:

$$
P_{i}V_{i}^{\gamma} = P_{f}V_{f}^{\gamma}
$$

We need to find the final volume, \(V_{f}\).

$$
P (9)^{3/2} = \left(\frac{27P}{8}\right) V_{f}^{3/2}
$$

Cancel the initial pressure \(P\) from both sides:

$$
(9)^{3/2} = \frac{27}{8} V_{f}^{3/2}
$$

Calculate \((9)^{3/2}\):

$$
(9)^{3/2} = (\sqrt{9})^{3} = 3^{3} = 27
$$

Now substitute this back into the equation:

$$
27 = \frac{27}{8} V_{f}^{3/2}
$$

Divide both sides by 27:

$$
1 = \frac{1}{8} V_{f}^{3/2}
$$

$$
V_{f}^{3/2} = 8
$$

To find \(V_{f}\), raise both sides to the power of \(2/3\):

$$
V_{f} = 8^{2/3} = (8^{1/3})^{2} = (2)^{2} = 4
$$

The final volume in the right-hand side compartment is 4 litres.

questions.question: 31. A poly-atomic molecule ($C_{V} = 3R$, $C_{P} = 4R$, where R is gas constant) goes from phase space point $A(P_{A} = 10^{5} \text{ Pa}, V_{A} = 4 \times 10^{-6} \text{m}^{3})$ to point $B (P_{B} = 5 \times 10^{4} \text{ Pa}, V_{B} = 6 \times 10^{-6} \text{m}^{3})$ to point $C (P_{C} = 10^{4} \text{ Pa}, V_{C} = 8 \times 10^{-6} \text{m}^{3})$. A to B is an adiabatic path and B to C is an isothermal path. The net heat absorbed per unit mole by the system is :
questions.explanation:
For the adiabatic process from A to B, the heat absorbed is zero.

$$
\Delta Q_{AB} = 0 \text{ (adiabatic)}
$$

For the isothermal process from B to C, the change in internal energy is zero (\(\Delta U = 0\)). Therefore, the heat absorbed is equal to the work done by the gas.

$$
\Delta Q_{BC} = \Delta W_{BC}
$$

The work done during an isothermal expansion for n moles of gas is given by \(W = nRT \ln(V_{final}/V_{initial})\). Here, the process is from B to C at a constant temperature of 450 K, and we are considering one mole (n=1).

$$
\Delta Q_{BC} = nRT \ln \left( \frac{V_{C}}{V_{B}} \right) = 450R \ln \left( \frac{8 \times 10^{-6}}{6 \times 10^{-6}} \right)
$$

Simplifying the expression:

$$
= 450R \ln \left( \frac{4}{3} \right) = 450R (\ln4 - \ln3)
$$

The net heat absorbed by the system is the sum of the heat absorbed in both processes.

$$
\therefore \Delta Q = \Delta Q_{AB} + \Delta Q_{BC}
$$

$$
\Delta Q = 0 + 450 R (\ln4 - \ln3)
$$

questions.question: Using the given P-V diagram, the work done by an ideal gas along the path ABCD is-
questions.explanation:
The total work done along the path ABCD is the sum of the work done in each segment:

$$
W_{\mathrm{ABCD}} = W_{\mathrm{AB}} + W_{\mathrm{BC}} + W_{\mathrm{CD}}
$$

Path AB is an isobaric expansion from \((P_0, 2V_0)\) to \((P_0, 3V_0)\). The work done is:

$$
W_{\mathrm{AB}} = P_0 \Delta V = P_0 (3V_0 - 2V_0) = P_0V_0
$$

Path BC is an isochoric process (constant volume) from \((P_0, 3V_0)\) to \((2P_0, 3V_0)\). The work done is zero:

$$
W_{\mathrm{BC}} = 0
$$

Path CD is an isobaric compression from \((2P_0, 3V_0)\) to \((2P_0, V_0)\). The work done is:

$$
W_{\mathrm{CD}} = P \Delta V = 2P_0 (V_0 - 3V_0) = 2P_0 (-2V_0) = -4P_0V_0
$$

Summing the work done for each segment:

$$
W_{\mathrm{ABCD}} = P_0V_0 + 0 + (-4P_0V_0)
$$

$$
W_{\mathrm{ABCD}} = P_0V_0 - 4P_0V_0
$$

$$
W_{\mathrm{ABCD}} = -3P_0V_0
$$

questions.question: Heat is supplied to a diatomic gas at constant pressure. Then the ratio of $\Delta Q : \Delta U : \Delta W$ is $\underline{\hspace{1cm}}$ .
questions.explanation:
For a diatomic gas, the molar specific heat at constant pressure (\(C_{p}\)) and constant volume (\(C_{v}\)) are:

$$
C_{p} = \frac{7}{2}R
$$

$$
C_{v} = \frac{5}{2}R
$$

The heat supplied at constant pressure is given by:

$$
\Delta Q = nC_{p}\Delta T = n\left(\frac{7}{2}R\right)\Delta T = \frac{7}{2}nRT
$$

The change in internal energy is given by:

$$
\Delta U = nC_{v}\Delta T = n\left(\frac{5}{2}R\right)\Delta T = \frac{5}{2}nRT
$$

For a process at constant pressure, the work done is \(\Delta W = P\Delta V\). Using the ideal gas law \(PV = nRT\), for a constant pressure process, \(P\Delta V = nR\Delta T\). Therefore:

$$
\Delta W = nR\Delta T
$$

Now, we form the ratio using the expressions derived:

$$
\Delta Q : \Delta U : \Delta W = \frac{7}{2}nRT : \frac{5}{2}nRT : nRT
$$

To simplify the ratio, we can divide all terms by \(nRT\) and then multiply by 2:

$$
\left(\frac{7}{2}\right) : \left(\frac{5}{2}\right) : 1
$$

$$
7 : 5 : 2
$$

questions.question: A diatomic gas ($\gamma = 1.4$) does 200 J of work when it is expanded isobarically. The heat given to the gas in the process is:
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Given: For a diatomic gas, \(\gamma = 1.4\). Work done \(W = P\Delta V = 200\) J. The process is isobaric.

The heat given to the gas in an isobaric process is given by the first law of thermodynamics:

$$
Q = \Delta U + W
$$

Where \(\Delta U = nC_v\Delta T\) and \(W = P\Delta V\). So,

$$
Q = nC_v\Delta T + P\Delta V
$$

We know that for an ideal gas, \(C_v = \frac{R}{\gamma-1}\). Also, for an isobaric process, \(P\Delta V = nR\Delta T\), which implies \(n\Delta T = \frac{P\Delta V}{R}\).

Substitute these into the equation for \(Q\):

$$
Q = \left(\frac{P\Delta V}{R}\right) \left(\frac{R}{\gamma-1}\right) + P\Delta V
$$

$$
Q = \frac{P\Delta V}{\gamma-1} + P\Delta V
$$

$$
Q = P\Delta V \left(1 + \frac{1}{\gamma-1}\right)
$$

Now, substitute the given values: \(P\Delta V = 200\) J and \(\gamma = 1.4\).

$$
Q = 200 \left(1 + \frac{1}{1.4-1}\right)
$$

$$
Q = 200 \left(1 + \frac{1}{0.4}\right)
$$

$$
Q = 200 (1 + 2.5)
$$

$$
Q = 200 \times 3.5
$$

$$
Q = 700 \text{ J}
$$

Thus, the heat given to the gas in the process is 700 J.

questions.question: A gas mixture consists of 8 moles of argon and 6 moles of oxygen at temperature T. Neglecting all vibrational modes, the total internal energy of the system is:
questions.explanation:
The internal energy of a gas is given by \(u = nC_{v}T\).

For a mixture of gases, the total internal energy is the sum of the internal energies of individual gases:

$$
u = n_{1}C_{v1}T + n_{2}C_{v2}T
$$

For Argon (monoatomic gas), neglecting vibrational modes, the molar specific heat at constant volume is \(C_{v1} = \frac{3}{2}R\).

For Oxygen (diatomic gas), neglecting vibrational modes, the molar specific heat at constant volume is \(C_{v2} = \frac{5}{2}R\).

Given:

• Moles of Argon (\(n_{1}\)) = 8 moles
• Moles of Oxygen (\(n_{2}\)) = 6 moles

Substituting these values into the equation for total internal energy:

$$
u = 8 \times \frac{3}{2} RT + 6 \times \frac{5}{2} RT
$$

$$
u = 12RT + 15RT
$$

$$
u = 27RT
$$

questions.question: An ideal gas has undergone through the cyclic process as shown in the figure. Work done by the gas in the entire cycle is ______ $ \times 10^{-1} $ J. (Take $ \pi = 3.14 $)
questions.explanation:
The given figure is a P-V diagram representing a cyclic process. The work done by the gas in a cyclic process is equal to the area enclosed by the cycle on the P-V diagram. In this case, the cycle is a circle.

For an elliptical or circular path on a P-V diagram, the work done \(W\) is given by the area of the ellipse/circle. If \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) are the diameters along the pressure and volume axes respectively, the area of the circle is \( \frac{\pi}{4} d_{1}d_{2} \).

$$
W = \frac{\pi}{4} d_{1}d_{2}
$$

• Diameter along the pressure axis (\(d_1\)): \(500 \text{ kPa} - 300 \text{ kPa} = 200 \text{ kPa}\)
• Diameter along the volume axis (\(d_2\)): \(350 \text{ cm}^3 - 150 \text{ cm}^3 = 200 \text{ cm}^3\)

Convert units to SI: \(1 \text{ kPa} = 10^3 \text{ Pa}\) and \(1 \text{ cm}^3 = 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3\).

$$
W = \frac{\pi}{4} (200 \times 10^3 \text{ Pa}) (200 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3)
$$

$$
W = \frac{3.14}{4} (200 \times 10^3) (200 \times 10^{-6})
$$

$$
W = \frac{3.14}{4} \times 40000 \times 10^{-3}
$$

$$
W = 3.14 \times 10000 \times 10^{-3}
$$

$$
W = 3.14 \times 10
$$

$$
W = 31.4 \text{ Joule}
$$

The question asks for the work done in the format \( \text{______} \times 10^{-1} \text{ J} \).

$$
W = 31.4 \text{ J} = 314 \times 10^{-1} \text{ J}
$$

questions.question: A gas is kept in a container having walls which are thermally non-conducting. Initially the gas has a volume of 800 $cm^3$ and temperature $27^\circ C$. The change in temperature when the gas is adiabatically compressed to 200 $cm^3$ is : (Take $\gamma = 1.5$ : $\gamma$ is the ratio of specific heats at constant pressure and at constant volume)
questions.explanation:
Given:

$$
V_1 = 800 \text{ cm}^3
$$

$$
V_2 = 200 \text{ cm}^3
$$

$$
T_1 = 27^\circ C = (27 + 273) \text{ K} = 300 \text{ K}
$$

$$
\gamma = 1.5
$$

For an adiabatic process, the relation between temperature and volume is:

$$
TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{constant}
$$

So, we can write:

$$
T_1 V_1^{\gamma-1} = T_2 V_2^{\gamma-1}
$$

Substitute the given values:

$$
(300 \text{ K}) (800 \text{ cm}^3)^{1.5-1} = T_2 (200 \text{ cm}^3)^{1.5-1}
$$

$$
300 \times (800)^{0.5} = T_2 \times (200)^{0.5}
$$

Solve for \(T_2\):

$$
T_2 = 300 \left(\frac{800}{200}\right)^{0.5}
$$

$$
T_2 = 300 \times (4)^{0.5}
$$

$$
T_2 = 300 \times 2
$$

$$
T_2 = 600 \text{ K}
$$

The question asks for the change in temperature (\(\Delta T\)):

$$
\Delta T = T_2 - T_1
$$

$$
\Delta T = 600 \text{ K} - 300 \text{ K}
$$

$$
\Delta T = 300 \text{ K}
$$

questions.question: Identify the characteristics of an adiabatic process in a monoatomic gas. (A) Internal energy is constant. (B) Work done in the process is equal to the change in internal energy. (C) The product of temperature and volume is a constant. (D) The product of pressure and volume is a constant. (E) The work done to change the temperature from $T_{1}$ to $T_{2}$ is proportional to $(T_{2} - T_{1})$ Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation:
For an adiabatic process, the heat exchange with the surroundings is zero, i.e., \(Q = 0\). According to the first law of thermodynamics:

$$
Q = \Delta U + W
$$

Since \(Q = 0\),

$$
0 = \Delta U + W \Rightarrow W = -\Delta U
$$

This means the work done by the gas is equal to the decrease in its internal energy. So, statement (B) is correct, interpreting 'equal to' as referring to the magnitude or the relationship between work and change in internal energy.

The work done in an adiabatic process is also given by:

$$
W = -nC_{V}\Delta T
$$

Where \(\Delta T = T_{2} - T_{1}\). From this equation, we can see that the work done (WD) is directly proportional to the change in temperature \((T_{2} - T_{1})\). Therefore, statement (E) is correct.

$$
|WD| = nC_{V}\Delta T \propto T_{2} - T_{1}
$$

Statement (A) is incorrect because in an adiabatic process, temperature changes, so internal energy (which depends on temperature) is not constant. This is a characteristic of an isothermal process.

Statements (C) and (D) are incorrect. For an adiabatic process, \(PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}\) and \(TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{constant}\), not \(PV = \text{constant}\) or \(TV = \text{constant}\).

Thus, the only correct statements are (B) and (E).

questions.question: The initial pressure and volume of an ideal gas are $P_0$ and $V_0$. The final pressure of the gas when the gas is suddenly compressed to volume $\frac{V_0}{4}$ will be : (Given $\gamma = \text{ratio of specific heats at constant pressure and at constant volume}$)
questions.explanation:
As the gas is suddenly compressed, the process is adiabatic. The equation of state for an adiabatic process is:

$$
PV^{\gamma} = \text{constant}
$$

Let the initial pressure and volume be \(P_0\) and \(V_0\), and the final pressure and volume be \(P_2\) and \(\frac{V_0}{4}\) respectively.

$$
P_0 V_0^{\gamma} = P_2 \left(\frac{V_0}{4}\right)^{\gamma}
$$

$$
P_2 = P_0 \frac{V_0^{\gamma}}{\left(\frac{V_0}{4}\right)^{\gamma}}
$$

$$
P_2 = P_0 \frac{V_0^{\gamma}}{V_0^{\gamma}/4^{\gamma}}
$$

$$
P_2 = P_0 (4)^{\gamma}
$$

questions.question: A piston of mass M is hung from a massless spring whose restoring force law goes as $F = -kx^3$, where k is the spring constant of appropriate dimension. The piston separates the vertical chamber into two parts, where the bottom part is filled with 'n' moles of an ideal gas. An external work is done on the gas isothermally (at a constant temperature T) with the help of a heating filament (with negligible volume) mounted in lower part of the chamber, so that the piston goes up from a height $L_0$ to $L_1$, the total energy delivered by the filament is (Assume spring to be in its natural length before heating)
questions.explanation:
### Using WET

Total energy supplied = gravitational potential energy + spring potential energy + work done by gas

$$
Mg (L_1 - L_0) + \int_{L_0}^{L_1} kx^3 dx + nRT \ln \left[\frac{L_1 A}{L_0 A}\right] + W_{ext} = 0
$$

Evaluating the integral and simplifying the logarithmic term:

$$
\frac{k}{4} [x^4]_{L_0}^{L_1} + Mg (L_1 - L_0) + nRT \ln \left[\frac{L_1}{L_0}\right] + W_{ext} = 0
$$

Where \(W_{ext}\) is the work done by the system on the filament. The energy delivered by the filament is \(Q = -W_{ext}\). Rearranging the equation to solve for \(Q\):

$$
Q = Mg (L_1 - L_0) + \frac{k}{4}(L_1^4 - L_0^4) + nRT \ln \left[\frac{L_1}{L_0}\right]
$$

questions.question: Two moles a monoatomic gas is mixed with six moles of a diatomic gas. The molar specific heat of the mixture at constant volume is:
questions.explanation:
For a monoatomic gas, the molar specific heat at constant volume is \(C_{v_1} = \frac{3}{2}R\).

For a diatomic gas, the molar specific heat at constant volume is \(C_{v_2} = \frac{5}{2}R\).

Given:

• Number of moles of monoatomic gas, \(n_1 = 2\)
• Number of moles of diatomic gas, \(n_2 = 6\)

The molar specific heat of the mixture at constant volume is given by the formula:

$$
C_{v_{mix}} = \frac{n_1 C_{v_1} + n_2 C_{v_2}}{n_1 + n_2}
$$

Substitute the given values into the formula:

$$
C_{v_{mix}} = \frac{2 \times \frac{3R}{2} + 6 \times \frac{5R}{2}}{2 + 6}
$$

$$
C_{v_{mix}} = \frac{3R + 15R}{8}
$$

$$
C_{v_{mix}} = \frac{18R}{8}
$$

Simplify the expression:

$$
C_{v_{mix}} = \frac{9R}{4}
$$

The ratio of final pressure and initial pressure is: ($\gamma$ is the ratio of specific heats of the gas at constant pressure and at constant volume)

questions.question: If 2 mole of an ideal monoatomic gas at temperature T, is mixed with 6 mole of another ideal monoatomic gas at temperature 2T then the temperature of mixture is :
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

The temperature of a mixture of ideal gases is given by the formula:

$$
T_{\text{mix}} = \frac{n_{1}C_{1}T_{1} + n_{2}C_{2}T_{2}}{n_{1}C_{1} + n_{2}C_{2}}
$$

For an ideal monoatomic gas, the molar specific heat at constant volume is \(C_{V} = \frac{3}{2}R\). Since the problem involves mixing and finding the final temperature, we use \(C_{V}\) for the internal energy calculation.

Given:

• First gas: \(n_{1} = 2\) mole, \(T_{1} = T\)
• Second gas: \(n_{2} = 6\) mole, \(T_{2} = 2T\)
• For monoatomic gas: \(C_{1} = C_{2} = \frac{3}{2}R\)

Substitute these values into the mixture temperature formula:

$$
T_{\text{mix}} = \frac{\left(2 \times \frac{3}{2}R \times T\right) + \left(6 \times \frac{3}{2}R \times 2T\right)}{\left(2 \times \frac{3}{2}R\right) + \left(6 \times \frac{3}{2}R\right)}
$$

Simplify the numerator and the denominator:

$$
T_{\text{mix}} = \frac{(3RT) + (18RT)}{(3R) + (9R)}
$$

$$
T_{\text{mix}} = \frac{21RT}{12R}
$$

Cancel out R from numerator and denominator, and simplify the fraction:

$$
T_{\text{mix}} = \frac{21T}{12} = \frac{7}{4}T
$$

Thus, the temperature of the mixture is \(\frac{7}{4}T\).

questions.question: The volume of an ideal gas increases 8 times and temperature becomes $(1/4)^{\text{th}}$ of initial temperature during a reversible change. If there is no exchange of heat in this process $(\Delta Q = 0)$ then identify the gas from the following options (Assuming the gases given in the options are ideal gases) :
questions.explanation:
For an adiabatic process, the relation between temperature and volume is given by:

$$
TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{constant}
$$

Given that the volume increases 8 times, so \(V_2 = 8V_1\).

And the temperature becomes \((1/4)^{\text{th}}\) of initial temperature, so \(T_2 = \frac{T_1}{4}\).

Applying the adiabatic relation:

$$
T_1 V_1^{\gamma-1} = T_2 V_2^{\gamma-1}
$$

$$
T_1 V_1^{\gamma-1} = \left(\frac{T_1}{4}\right) (8V_1)^{\gamma-1}
$$

Dividing both sides by \(T_1 V_1^{\gamma-1}\):

$$
1 = \frac{1}{4} (8)^{\gamma-1}
$$

$$
4 = 8^{\gamma-1}
$$

Expressing both sides with base 2:

$$
2^2 = (2^3)^{\gamma-1}
$$

$$
2^2 = 2^{3(\gamma-1)}
$$

Equating the exponents:

$$
2 = 3(\gamma-1)
$$

$$
2 = 3\gamma - 3
$$

$$
5 = 3\gamma
$$

$$
\gamma = \frac{5}{3}
$$

The value of \(\gamma = 5/3\) corresponds to a monoatomic gas.

Among the given options, Helium (He) is a monoatomic gas.

questions.question: 0.  08 kg air is heated at constant volume through 5°C. The specific heat of air at constant volume is 0.17 kcal/kg °C and J = 4.18 joule/cal. The change in its internal energy is approximately

Match List I with List II
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

items.label: I
items.text: Work done by the gas decreases internal energy

items.label: III
items.text: The heat absorbed goes partly to increase internal energy and partly to do work

items.label: IV
items.text: No work is done on or by the gas

questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

An Isothermal process is one where the temperature of the system remains constant. For an ideal gas, internal energy \(u\) depends only on temperature. Therefore, for an isothermal process, the change in internal energy is zero: \(\Delta u = 0\). This matches List II - II.

So, A \(\rightarrow\) II.

An Adiabatic process is one where no heat is exchanged with the surroundings, meaning \(\Delta Q = 0\). According to the First Law of Thermodynamics, \(\Delta u = \Delta Q - \Delta w\). Since \(\Delta Q = 0\), we have \(\Delta u = -\Delta w\). If work is done by the gas (\(\Delta w > 0\)), then \(\Delta u < 0\), which means the internal energy decreases. This matches List II - I.

So, B \(\rightarrow\) I.

An Isochoric process is one where the volume of the system remains constant, so \(\Delta V = 0\). The work done by the gas is given by \(\Delta w = P\Delta V\). Since \(\Delta V = 0\), no work is done on or by the gas (\(\Delta w = 0\)). This matches List II - IV.

So, C \(\rightarrow\) IV.

An Isobaric process is one where the pressure of the system remains constant. In this process, both volume and temperature can change, so both \(\Delta u \neq 0\) and \(\Delta w \neq 0\). The heat absorbed (\(\Delta Q\)) is used partly to increase the internal energy (\(\Delta u\)) and partly to do work (\(\Delta w\)) against the constant external pressure, as per \(\Delta Q = \Delta u + \Delta w\). This matches List II - III.

So, D \(\rightarrow\) III.

Based on the analysis, the correct matching is:

• A. Isothermal Process \(\rightarrow\) II. No change in internal energy
• B. Adiabatic Process \(\rightarrow\) I. Work done by the gas decreases internal energy
• C. Isochoric Process \(\rightarrow\) IV. No work is done on or by the gas
• D. Isobaric Process \(\rightarrow\) III. The heat absorbed goes partly to increase internal energy and partly to do work

This corresponds to option (2) in the given choices.

questions.question: Water of mass $m$ gram is slowly heated to increase the temperature from $T_{1}$ to $T_{2}$. The change in entropy of the water, given specific heat of water is $1\ Jkg^{-1}K^{-1}$, is :
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

The infinitesimal heat absorbed by a substance of mass \(m\) and specific heat \(s\) for an infinitesimal temperature change \(dT\) is given by:

$$
dQ = msdT
$$

The infinitesimal change in entropy \(dS\) is defined as the infinitesimal heat absorbed divided by the absolute temperature \(T\):

$$
dS = \frac{dQ}{T} = \frac{msdT}{T}
$$

To find the total change in entropy \(\Delta S\) when the temperature changes from \(T_{1}\) to \(T_{2}\), we integrate \(dS\):

$$
\Delta S = \int_{T_{1}}^{T_{2}} \frac{msdT}{T}
$$

Assuming \(m\) and \(s\) are constant over the temperature range:

$$
\Delta S = ms \int_{T_{1}}^{T_{2}} \frac{dT}{T} = ms [\ln T]_{T_{1}}^{T_{2}}
$$

$$
\Delta S = ms (\ln T_{2} - \ln T_{1}) = ms \ln \left(\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}\right)
$$

Given that the specific heat of water \(s = 1\ Jkg^{-1}K^{-1}\). Substituting this value:

$$
\Delta S = m(1) \ln \left(\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}\right) = m \ln \left(\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}\right)
$$

Thus, the change in entropy is \(m \ln \left(\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}\right)\).

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Statement I : If heat is added to a system, its temperature must increase. Statement II : If positive work is done by a system in a thermodynamic process, its volume must increase. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.explanation:
Statement I: If heat is added to a system, its temperature must increase.

This statement is False. For example, in an isothermal process, heat can be added to the system, but its temperature remains constant. Also, during a phase change (e.g., melting ice at 0°C), heat is added, but the temperature does not increase until the phase change is complete.

Statement II: If positive work is done by a system in a thermodynamic process, its volume must increase.

This statement is True. The work done by a system is given by \(W = \int PdV\). If the work done by the system (W) is positive, it implies that the change in volume (dV) must be positive, meaning the volume of the system increases.

Therefore, Statement I is false, and Statement II is true.

questions.question: A sample of gas at temperature T is adiabatically expanded to double its volume. The work done by the gas in the process is (given, $\gamma = \frac{3}{2}$) :
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Work done in an adiabatic process is given by:

$$
W = \frac{R}{\gamma - 1}(T_1 - T_2)
$$

For an adiabatic process, the relation between temperature and volume is:

$$
T_1 V_1^{\gamma - 1} = T_2 V_2^{\gamma - 1}
$$

Given initial temperature \(T_1 = T\), initial volume \(V_1 = V\), final volume \(V_2 = 2V\), and \(\gamma = \frac{3}{2}\). Substituting these values:

$$
TV^{\frac{3}{2} - 1} = T_2(2V)^{\frac{3}{2} - 1}
$$

$$
TV^{\frac{1}{2}} = T_2(2V)^{\frac{1}{2}}
$$

$$
T^2V = T_2^2 \times 2V
$$

$$
T_2^2 = \frac{T^2V}{2V} = \frac{T^2}{2}
$$

$$
\therefore T_2 = \frac{T}{\sqrt{2}}
$$

Now, substitute \(T_2\) and \(\gamma\) into the work done equation:

$$
W = \frac{R}{\frac{3}{2} - 1} \times \left(T - \frac{T}{\sqrt{2}}\right)
$$

$$
W = \frac{R}{\frac{1}{2}} \times T \left(1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)
$$

$$
= 2RT \left[1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right]
$$

$$
= RT \left[2 - \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\right]
$$

$$
= RT[2 - \sqrt{2}]
$$

questions.question: In the following $p-V$ diagram the equation of state along the curved path is given by $(V - 2)^2 = 4ap$ where $a$ is a constant. The total work done in the closed path is
questions.explanation:
The work done in a closed \(p-V\) cycle is equal to the area enclosed by the loop. For a clockwise cycle, the work done by the gas is negative. The given curve \((V - 2)^2 = 4ap\) is a parabola opening along the \(p\)-axis with its vertex at \((V=2, p=0)\). The area enclosed by the cycle A-B-C-A can be calculated as the area of the parabolic segment.

The area of a parabolic segment is \(\frac{2}{3}\) of the area of the circumscribing rectangle. In this case, the rectangle AC31A has a base of \((3-1) = 2\) and a height of \(P_0\).

$$
w = \text{Area of parabola} = \frac{2}{3} \text{ (Area of rectangle AC31A)}
$$

$$
= \frac{2}{3} P_0 (3-1) = \frac{4P_0}{3}
$$

From the diagram, at \(V=1\), the pressure is \(P_0\). Substitute \(V=1\) and \(p=P_0\) into the given equation of state:

$$
(1-2)^2 = 4aP_0
$$

$$
(-1)^2 = 4aP_0
$$

$$
1 = 4aP_0
$$

$$
P_0 = \frac{1}{4a}
$$

Substitute the value of \(P_0\) back into the expression for work done:

$$
w = \frac{4}{3} P_0 = \frac{4}{3} \left(\frac{1}{4a}\right) = \frac{1}{3a}
$$

Since the cycle is clockwise on the \(p-V\) diagram, the work done by the gas is negative.

questions.question: 1 g of a liquid is converted to vapour at $3 \times 10^5$ Pa pressure. If 10% of the heat supplied is used for increasing the volume by $1600 \text{ cm}^3$ during this phase change, then the increase in internal energy in the process will be:
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Given that 10% of the heat supplied (\(\Delta Q\)) is used for increasing the volume, which is the work done (W) by the gas.

$$
W = P \Delta V
$$

Also, \(W = \frac{10}{100} \Delta Q = \frac{\Delta Q}{10}\).

Given pressure \(P = 3 \times 10^5\) Pa and increase in volume \(\Delta V = 1600 \text{ cm}^3\).

Convert volume to \(\text{m}^3\): \(1600 \text{ cm}^3 = 1600 \times (10^{-2} \text{ m})^3 = 1600 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3\).

Now, calculate the work done:

$$
\frac{\Delta Q}{10} = P \Delta V = (3 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}) \times (1600 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3)
$$

$$
\frac{\Delta Q}{10} = 3 \times 10^5 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-3} = 4.8 \times 10^2 = 480 \text{ J}
$$

From this, we can find the total heat supplied \(\Delta Q\):

$$
\Delta Q = 10 \times 480 \text{ J} = 4800 \text{ J}
$$

Using the first law of thermodynamics:

$$
\Delta Q = \Delta u + W
$$

Substitute \(W = \frac{\Delta Q}{10}\) into the equation:

$$
\Delta Q = \Delta u + \frac{\Delta Q}{10}
$$

Rearrange to find the increase in internal energy \(\Delta u\):

$$
\Delta u = \Delta Q - \frac{\Delta Q}{10} = \frac{9}{10} \Delta Q
$$

Substitute the value of \(\Delta Q\):

$$
\Delta u = \frac{9}{10} \times 4800 \text{ J}
$$

$$
\Delta u = 9 \times 480 \text{ J} = 4320 \text{ J}
$$

questions.question: Pressure of an ideal gas, contained in a closed vessel, is increased by 0.4% when heated by 1$^{\circ}$C. Its initial temperature must be :
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

The gas is contained in a closed vessel, implying a constant volume. Therefore, it is an isochoric process.

For an ideal gas in an isochoric process, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature (Gay-Lussac's Law):

$$
P \propto T
$$

From the proportionality, the fractional change in pressure is equal to the fractional change in absolute temperature:

$$
\frac{\Delta P}{P} = \frac{\Delta T}{T}
$$

Given that the pressure is increased by 0.4%, so \(\frac{\Delta P}{P} = \frac{0.4}{100}\). The temperature is heated by 1\(^{\circ}\)C, which means \(\Delta T = 1\) K (since a change of 1\(^{\circ}\)C is equal to a change of 1 K).

Substituting these values into the equation:

$$
\frac{0.4}{100} = \frac{1}{T}
$$

Now, solve for T:

$$
T = \frac{100}{0.4}
$$

$$
T = \frac{1000}{4}
$$

$$
T = 250 \text{ K}
$$

The initial temperature must be 250 K.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: One is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R. Assertion A: If $dQ$ and $dW$ represent the heat supplied to the system and the work done on the system respectively. Then according to the first law of thermodynamics $dQ = dU - dW$. Reason R: First law of thermodynamics is based on law of conservation of energy. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
A is not correct but R is correct
A is correct but R is not correct
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
questions.explanation:
First law of thermodynamics is based on energy conservation.

The standard equation is:

$$
dQ = dU + dW
$$

where \(dW\) is the work done by the system.

In the question, \(dW\) is defined as work done on the system. Work done on the system is the negative of work done by the system.

So, \(dW_{\text{by system}} = -dW_{\text{on system}}\). Let's use the symbol \(dW'\) for work done on the system as given in the assertion.

$$
dW_{\text{by system}} = -dW'
$$

Substituting this into the standard equation:

$$
dQ = dU + (-dW')
$$

$$
dQ = dU - dW'
$$

This matches the expression given in Assertion A. Thus, Assertion A is correct.

Reason R states that the first law is based on energy conservation, which is a correct fundamental statement.

Since the first law is the mathematical formulation of energy conservation for a thermodynamic system, Reason R is the correct explanation for Assertion A.

questions.question: Initial pressure and volume of a monoatomic ideal gas are P and V. The change in internal energy of this gas in adiabatic expansion to volume $V_{\text{final}} = 27 V$ is $ $ J.
questions.explanation:
For an adiabatic process, we have \(P_1V_1^{\gamma} = P_2V_2^{\gamma}\). For a monoatomic ideal gas, the adiabatic index \(\gamma = \frac{5}{3}\).

$$
PV^{5/3} = P_2 \times (27V)^{5/3}
$$

$$
P_2 = \frac{P}{(27)^{5/3}} = \frac{P}{(3^3)^{5/3}} = \frac{P}{3^5}
$$

The change in internal energy for an ideal gas in an adiabatic process is given by:

Substitute the values of \(P_1, V_1, P_2, V_2\) and \(\gamma\):

$$
\Delta U = \frac{\left(\frac{P}{3^5}\right) (27V) - PV}{\frac{5}{3}-1}
$$

$$
\Delta U = \frac{\left(\frac{P}{3^5}\right) (3^3V) - PV}{\frac{2}{3}}
$$

$$
\Delta U = \frac{\frac{P}{3^2}V - PV}{\frac{2}{3}}
$$

$$
\Delta U = \frac{\frac{PV}{9} - PV}{\frac{2}{3}}
$$

$$
\Delta U = \frac{PV\left(\frac{1}{9} - 1\right)}{\frac{2}{3}}
$$

$$
\Delta U = \frac{PV\left(-\frac{8}{9}\right)}{\frac{2}{3}}
$$

$$
\Delta U = -PV \times \frac{8}{9} \times \frac{3}{2}
$$

$$
\Delta U = -PV \times \frac{4}{3}
$$

$$
\Delta U = -\frac{4}{3}PV
$$

questions.question: The pressure and volume of an ideal gas are related as $PV^{\frac{3}{2}} = K(\text{Constant})$. The work done when the gas is taken from state A $(P_1, V_1, T_1)$ to state B $(P_2, V_2, T_2))$ is:
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

The given relation for an ideal gas is:

$$
PV^{\frac{3}{2}} = K
$$

This equation represents a polytropic process, where the exponent \(x = \frac{3}{2}\). The work done (WD) by the gas in a polytropic process from state A to state B is given by the formula:

$$
WD = \frac{P_2V_2 - P_1V_1}{1-x}
$$

Substituting the value of \(x = \frac{3}{2}\) into the formula:

$$
WD = \frac{P_2V_2 - P_1V_1}{1-\frac{3}{2}}
$$

$$
WD = \frac{P_2V_2 - P_1V_1}{-\frac{1}{2}}
$$

$$
WD = -2(P_2V_2 - P_1V_1)
$$

Distributing the negative sign, we get:

$$
WD = 2(P_1V_1 - P_2V_2)
$$

Therefore, the work done when the gas is taken from state A to state B is \(2(P_1V_1 - P_2V_2)\).

questions.explanation:
• Number of moles, \(n = 5\)

• Gas constant, \(R = 8.36 \text{ J/mol. } ^\circ\text{C}\)
• We need to find the change in internal energy, \(\Delta U\).

We know that \(1 \text{ calorie} \approx 4.18 \text{ Joules}\).

$$
R = \frac{8.36 \text{ J/mol. } ^\circ\text{C}}{4.18 \text{ J/cal}} = 2 \text{ cal/mol. } ^\circ\text{C}
$$

Mayer's relation states that \(c_{p} - c_{v} = R\).

$$
c_{v} = c_{p} - R = 8 \text{ cal/mol. } ^\circ\text{C} - 2 \text{ cal/mol. } ^\circ\text{C} = 6 \text{ cal/mol. } ^\circ\text{C}
$$

$$

For a gas heated at constant volume, the change in internal energy is given by:

$$
\Delta U = n c_{v} \Delta T
$$

$$
\Delta U = 5 \text{ mol} \times 6 \text{ cal/mol. } ^\circ\text{C} \times 10^\circ\text{C}
$$

$$
\Delta U = 300 \text{ cal}
$$

So heat will be used to do positive work.

Thus, statements C (Internal energy of the gas will not change) and D (The gas will do positive work) are correct.

questions.question: Heat energy of 735 J is given to a diatomic gas allowing the gas to expand at constant pressure. Each gas molecule rotates around an internal axis but do not oscillate. The increase in the internal energy of the gas will be :
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Given heat energy \(Q = 735\) J.

The process occurs at constant pressure.

The gas is diatomic, rotates around an internal axis but does not oscillate. This means it has 3 translational degrees of freedom and 2 rotational degrees of freedom.

Total degrees of freedom \(f = 3 \text{ (translational)} + 2 \text{ (rotational)} = 5\).

For a gas with \(f\) degrees of freedom, the molar specific heat at constant volume is \(C_v = \frac{f}{2}R\).

$$
C_v = \frac{5}{2}R
$$

The molar specific heat at constant pressure is \(C_p = C_v + R\).

$$
C_p = \frac{5}{2}R + R = \frac{7}{2}R
$$

The ratio of specific heats (\(\gamma\)) is \(\frac{C_p}{C_v}\).

$$
\gamma = \frac{C_p}{C_v} = \frac{7/2 R}{5/2 R} = \frac{7}{5}
$$

For a constant pressure process, the heat supplied \(Q = nC_p \Delta T\) and the change in internal energy \(\Delta U = nC_v \Delta T\).

We can relate \(\Delta U\) to \(Q\) using the ratio of specific heats:

$$
\Delta U = \frac{nC_v \Delta T}{nC_p \Delta T} \times Q = \frac{C_v}{C_p} \times Q = \frac{Q}{\gamma}
$$

Substitute the values:

$$
\Delta U = \frac{735 \text{ J}}{7/5} = \frac{735 \times 5}{7} \text{ J}
$$

$$
\Delta U = 105 \times 5 \text{ J} = 525 \text{ J}
$$

questions.question: A source supplies heat to a system at the rate of 1000 W. If the system performs work at a rate of 200 W. The rate at which internal energy of the system increase is
questions.explanation:
From 1st law of thermodynamics,

$$
dQ = dU + dW
$$

Also, we can write this as,

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt} = \frac{dU}{dt} + \frac{dW}{dt}
$$

Given:

Rate of heat supplied, \(\frac{dQ}{dt} = 1000\) W

Rate of work done by the system, \(\frac{dW}{dt} = 200\) W

Substituting these values into the equation:

$$
\Rightarrow 1000W = \frac{dU}{dt} + 200W
$$

To find the rate at which internal energy of the system increases (\(\frac{dU}{dt}\)), rearrange the equation:

$$
\Rightarrow \frac{dU}{dt} = 1000W - 200W
$$

$$
\Rightarrow \frac{dU}{dt} = 800W
$$

Thus, the rate at which the internal energy of the system increases is 800 W.

questions.question: A sample of 1 mole gas at temperature T is adiabatically expanded to double its volume. If adiabatic constant for the gas is $\gamma = \frac{3}{2}$, then the work done by the gas in the process is:
questions.explanation:
Given: Number of moles \(n = 1\), initial temperature \(T_1 = T\), initial volume \(V_1 = V\). The gas is expanded to double its volume, so final volume \(V_2 = 2V\). Adiabatic constant \(\gamma = \frac{3}{2}\).

For an adiabatic process, the relation between temperature and volume is \(T V^{\gamma-1} = \text{constant}\).

$$
T_1 V_1^{\gamma-1} = T_2 V_2^{\gamma-1}
$$

$$
T \times V^{\frac{3}{2}-1} = T_2 \times (2V)^{\frac{3}{2}-1}
$$

$$
T V^{\frac{1}{2}} = T_2 (2V)^{\frac{1}{2}}
$$

$$
T V^{\frac{1}{2}} = T_2 \sqrt{2} V^{\frac{1}{2}}
$$

$$
T = T_2 \sqrt{2}
$$

$$
T_2 = \frac{T}{\sqrt{2}}
$$

The work done (WD) by the gas in an adiabatic process is given by:

$$
WD = \frac{nR(T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1}
$$

Substitute the values \(n=1\), \(T_1=T\), \(T_2=\frac{T}{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(\gamma = \frac{3}{2}\):

$$
WD = \frac{1 \cdot R \left(T - \frac{T}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}{\frac{3}{2} - 1}
$$

$$
WD = \frac{R T \left(1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}{\frac{1}{2}}
$$

$$
WD = 2 R T \left(1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)
$$

$$
WD = 2 R T \left(\frac{\sqrt{2} - 1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)
$$

Multiply numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{2}\) to rationalize:

$$
WD = 2 R T \left(\frac{(\sqrt{2} - 1)\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{2}}\right)
$$

$$
WD = 2 R T \left(\frac{2 - \sqrt{2}}{2}\right)
$$

$$
WD = R T \left[2 - \sqrt{2}\right]
$$

questions.question: Density of water at $4^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $20^{\circ}\text{C}$ are $1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$ and $998\ \text{kg/m}^3$ respectively. The increase in internal energy of $4\ \text{kg}$ water when it is heated from $4^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $20^{\circ}\text{C}$ is $ \text{____} $ J. (Specific heat capacity of water = $4.2\ \text{J/kg}\cdot\text{K}$ and $1$ atmospheric pressure = $10^5\ \text{Pa}$)
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

The heat absorbed by the water is given by the formula \(Q = mS\Delta T\), where \(m\) is the mass, \(S\) is the specific heat capacity, and \(\Delta T\) is the change in temperature.

$$
m = 4\ \text{kg}
$$

$$
S = 4.2\ \text{J/kg}\cdot\text{K}
$$

$$
\Delta T = 20^{\circ}\text{C} - 4^{\circ}\text{C} = 16^{\circ}\text{C} = 16\ \text{K}
$$

$$
Q = 4 \times 4200 \times 16\ \text{J}
$$

$$
Q = 268800\ \text{J}
$$

The work done by the water against constant atmospheric pressure is given by \(W = P\Delta V\), where \(P\) is the pressure and \(\Delta V\) is the change in volume.

$$
P = 10^5\ \text{Pa}
$$

The change in volume \(\Delta V\) can be calculated from the mass and densities:

$$
\Delta V = V_{\text{final}} - V_{\text{initial}} = \frac{m}{\rho_{\text{final}}} - \frac{m}{\rho_{\text{initial}}} = m \left( \frac{1}{\rho_{\text{final}}} - \frac{1}{\rho_{\text{initial}}} \right)
$$

Given densities: \(\rho_{\text{initial}} = 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3\) (at \(4^{\circ}\text{C}\)) and \(\rho_{\text{final}} = 998\ \text{kg/m}^3\) (at \(20^{\circ}\text{C}\)).

$$
\Delta V = 4 \left( \frac{1}{998} - \frac{1}{1000} \right)
$$

$$
\Delta V = 4 \left( \frac{1000 - 998}{998 \times 1000} \right)
$$

$$
\Delta V = 4 \left( \frac{2}{998000} \right) = \frac{8}{998000}\ \text{m}^3
$$

$$
W = P\Delta V = 10^5 \times \frac{8}{998000}
$$

$$
W = \frac{8 \times 10^5}{998 \times 10^3} = \frac{800}{998} \approx 0.8016\ \text{J}
$$

Rounding to one decimal place as in the provided solution:

$$
W \approx 0.8\ \text{J}
$$

According to the First Law of Thermodynamics, the change in internal energy \(\Delta U\) is given by:

$$
\Delta U = Q - W
$$

$$
\Delta U = 268800\ \text{J} - 0.8\ \text{J}
$$

$$
\Delta U = 268799.2\ \text{J}
$$

questions.question: An ideal gas initially at $0^{\circ}C$ temperature, is compressed suddenly to one fourth of its volume. If the ratio of specific heat at constant pressure to that at constant volume is $3/2$, the change in temperature due to the thermodynamics process is _______ K.
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

$$
\gamma = \frac{3}{2}
$$

For an adiabatic process, the relation between temperature and volume is given by:

$$
TV^{\gamma-1} = C \quad (\text{constant})
$$

Given initial temperature \(T_{1} = 0^{\circ}C = 273\) K.

Let initial volume be \(V_{1} = V_{0}\).

Final volume \(V_{2} = \frac{V_{0}}{4}\).

Using the adiabatic relation:

$$
T_{1}V_{1}^{\gamma-1} = T_{2}V_{2}^{\gamma-1}
$$

$$
273 V_{0}^{\frac{3}{2}-1} = T_{2} \left(\frac{V_{0}}{4}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}-1}
$$

$$
273 V_{0}^{0.5} = T_{2} \left(\frac{V_{0}}{4}\right)^{0.5}
$$

$$
273 V_{0}^{0.5} = T_{2} \frac{V_{0}^{0.5}}{4^{0.5}}

273 = T_{2} \frac{1}{2}

$$
T_{2} = 273 \times 2 = 546 \text{ K}

$$

questions.question: A vessel contains $0.15 \text{ m}^3$ of a gas at pressure 8 bar and temperature $140^{\circ}\text{C}$ with $c_p = 3R$ and $c_v = 2R$. It is expanded adiabatically till pressure falls to 1 bar. The work done during this process is ______ kJ. (R is gas constant)
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

Given data:

• Initial volume, \(V_{1} = 0.15 \text{ m}^3\)
• Initial pressure, \(P_{1} = 8 \text{ bar} = 8 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}\)
• Final pressure, \(P_{2} = 1 \text{ bar} = 1 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}\)
• Specific heat at constant pressure, \(c_p = 3R\)
• Specific heat at constant volume, \(c_v = 2R\)

The adiabatic index \(\gamma\) is the ratio of specific heats:

$$
\gamma = \frac{c_p}{c_v} = \frac{3R}{2R} = \frac{3}{2} = 1.5
$$

For an adiabatic process, the relation between pressure and volume is given by:

$$
P_{1}V_{1}^{\gamma} = P_{2}V_{2}^{\gamma}
$$

Rearranging the equation to solve for \(V_{2}\):

$$
V_{2}^{\gamma} = \frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}} V_{1}^{\gamma} \Rightarrow V_{2} = \left( \frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}} \right)^{1/\gamma} V_{1}
$$

Substituting the given values:

$$
V_{2} = \left( \frac{8}{1} \right)^{1/1.5} \times 0.15 = (8)^{2/3} \times 0.15
$$

$$
V_{2} = (2^3)^{2/3} \times 0.15 = 2^2 \times 0.15 = 4 \times 0.15 = 0.6 \text{ m}^3
$$

The work done during an adiabatic process is given by the formula:

$$
W = \frac{P_{1}V_{1} - P_{2}V_{2}}{\gamma - 1}
$$

Substituting the values (remembering to convert bar to Pascals, \(1 \text{ bar} = 10^5 \text{ Pa}\)):

$$
W = \frac{(8 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}) \times (0.15 \text{ m}^3) - (1 \times 10^5 \text{ Pa}) \times (0.6 \text{ m}^3)}{1.5 - 1}
$$

$$
W = \frac{1.2 \times 10^5 - 0.6 \times 10^5}{0.5} = \frac{0.6 \times 10^5}{0.5} = 1.2 \times 10^5 \text{ J}
$$

The question asks for the work done in kilojoules (kJ). To convert from Joules to kilojoules, we divide by 1000:

$$
W = \frac{1.2 \times 10^5}{1000} \text{ kJ} = 120 \text{ kJ}
$$

questions.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion $A$ and the other is labelled as Reason $R$ Assertion $A$: Efficiency of a reversible heat engine will be highest at $-273^{\circ}C$ temperature of cold reservoir. Reason $R$: The efficiency of Carnot's engine depends not only on temperature of cold reservoir but it depends on the temperature of hot reservoir too and is given as $\eta = (1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1})$. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both $A$ and $R$ are true but $R$ is NOT the correct explanation of $A$
Both $A$ and $R$ are true and $R$ is the correct explanation of $A$
questions.explanation:
$$
\eta = 1 - \frac{T_L}{T_H} = \frac{T_H - T_L}{T_H}
$$

Efficiency of Carnot's engine will be highest at \(-273^{\circ} = 0K\)

Both Assertion A and Reason R are true, and Reason R correctly explains Assertion A. The efficiency of a Carnot engine is given by \(\eta = 1 - \frac{T_L}{T_H}\), where \(T_L\) is the temperature of the cold reservoir and \(T_H\) is the temperature of the hot reservoir. For the efficiency to be highest (ideally 100%), \(T_L\) must be \(0K\) (or \(-273^{\circ}C\)). Reason R correctly states that efficiency depends on both \(T_L\) and \(T_H\) and provides the correct formula, which directly supports Assertion A.

questions.question: A Carnot engine (E) is working between two temperatures 473K and 273K. In a new system two engines – engine $E_{1}$ works between 473K to 373K and engine $E_{2}$ works between 373K to 273K. If $\eta_{12}$, $\eta_{1}$ and $\eta_{2}$ are the efficiencies of the engines E, $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$, respectively, then
questions.explanation:
The efficiency of a Carnot engine is given by \(\eta = 1 - \frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}\), where \(T_{C}\) is the cold reservoir temperature and \(T_{H}\) is the hot reservoir temperature.

Engine E works between \(T_{H} = 473K\) and \(T_{C} = 273K\).

$$
\eta_{12} = 1 - \frac{273}{473} = \frac{473 - 273}{473} = \frac{200}{473} \approx 0.423
$$

Engine \(E_{1}\) works between \(T_{H} = 473K\) and \(T_{C} = 373K\).

$$
\eta_1 = 1 - \frac{373}{473} = \frac{473 - 373}{473} = \frac{100}{473} \approx 0.211
$$

Engine \(E_{2}\) works between \(T_{H} = 373K\) and \(T_{C} = 273K\).

$$
\eta_2 = 1 - \frac{273}{373} = \frac{373 - 273}{373} = \frac{100}{373} \approx 0.268
$$

Now, let's find the sum of the efficiencies of \(E_{1}\) and \(E_{2}\):

$$
\eta_1 + \eta_2 \approx 0.211 + 0.268 = 0.479
$$

Comparing \(\eta_{12}\) with \(\eta_1 + \eta_2\):

$$
0.423 < 0.479
$$

Therefore, \(\eta_{12} < \eta_1 + \eta_2\).

This corresponds to option (1).

questions.question: 10 mole of an ideal gas is undergoing the process shown in the figure. The heat involved in the process from $P_{1}$ to $P_{2}$ is $\alpha$ Joule ($P_{1} = 21.7$ Pa and $P_{2} = 30$ Pa, $C_{v} = 21$ J/K.mol, $R = 8.3$ J/mol.K). The value of $\alpha$ is $ \_\_\_\_ $.
questions.explanation:
The process from \(P_{1}\) to \(P_{2}\) shown in the figure is an isochoric process, meaning the volume \(V\) remains constant. From the graph, the constant volume is \(V = 1\) m\(^{3}\). The heat involved in an isochoric process is given by:

$$
\Delta Q = nC_{v}\Delta T
$$

Using the ideal gas law, \(PV = nRT\), we can write \(nR\Delta T = \Delta (PV) = V\Delta P\) (since \(V\) is constant). Therefore, \(\Delta T = \frac{V\Delta P}{nR}\).

Substitute this into the heat formula:

$$
\Delta Q = nC_{v} \left( \frac{V\Delta P}{nR} \right) = \frac{C_{v}}{R} V\Delta P
$$

Here, \(\Delta P = P_{2} - P_{1}\).

Given values are:

• \(C_{v} = 21\) J/K.mol
• \(R = 8.3\) J/mol.K
• \(P_{1} = 21.7\) Pa
• \(P_{2} = 30\) Pa
• \(V = 1\) m\(^{3}\)

Now, substitute these values into the derived formula:

$$
\Delta Q = \frac{21}{8.3} \times (30 - 21.7) \times 1
$$

$$
